title: How often should you change your pad?
description: Learn how often to change your pad, when to change sooner, and what to check for overnight pads and liners, with links to CDC and ACOG guidance.
imageAlt: Pink Mochi beside a sanitary pad and a purple alarm clock
intro: Change your pad every few hours, sooner if it feels full, wet or uncomfortable. Follow the instructions for your product and adjust to your flow. A reminder can help you check in, but you can change your pad before it rings.

paragraphs.first: The CDC recommends changing sanitary pads every few hours, including on light-flow days. ACOG describes changing them at least every 4 to 8 hours, or sooner when they feel full, wet or uncomfortable. These are general guidelines, not a reason to wait if you need a fresh pad.
paragraphs.second: On heavier days, check more often. Choose the absorbency that suits your flow, and follow the instructions on the packet.

table.caption: A practical guide to pads and liners
rows: Change sooner for heavier flow or discomfort.
Use a fresh one before bed; change when you wake or sooner if needed.

paragraphs.first: Choose a product intended for overnight use and follow its wear-time instructions. Put on a fresh one before bed and change it when you wake, or sooner if it is full or uncomfortable.
paragraphs.second: An overnight label is not a universal promise that every pad can be worn for the same number of hours. If you regularly need to change products very frequently because of heavy bleeding, ask a healthcare professional for advice.

paragraphs.first: Liners are thinner products for light flow or spotting. Change them regularly and whenever they feel damp or uncomfortable. For heavier bleeding, use a product suited to that flow.

items.full: The pad feels full, wet or uncomfortable.
items.leaks: You notice a leak or the product has shifted.
items.time: It is time to change according to the product instructions, even if your flow is light.

paragraphs.first: Mochi has an optional pad change reminder with a countdown in the Dynamic Island and on the Lock Screen. Its published feature information describes day pad, overnight pad and liner options, with a duration you choose.
paragraphs.second: A timer is a prompt to check your product, not a measure of how full it is or proof that a chosen interval is right for you. Change sooner whenever needed.

hours.question: Can I keep a pad on just because the timer has not finished?
hours.answer: Change it sooner if it feels full, wet or uncomfortable. Follow the product instructions. A timer cannot assess your flow or the condition of the pad.

light.question: Do I still need to change my pad if my flow is light?
light.answer: Yes. The CDC advises changing pads every few hours even when the flow is light, and more frequently for heavier bleeding.

night.question: Does every overnight pad have the same wear time?
night.answer: No single interval applies to every product. Choose a product intended for overnight use and follow its instructions. Change it sooner if it feels full or uncomfortable.
